651.event: After seven people in the Chicago area died in September 1982 from Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with cyanide, Johnson & Johnson's subsidiary McNeil Consumer Products carried out what was then the largest consumer product recall in American history, about 31 million bottles. Chairman James Burke said the recall and replacement would cost over 100 million dollars and that none of it would be passed on to customers. In November 1982 the company became the first to return to the market with the new tamper-resistant packaging required by the Food and Drug Administration, offering to replace any bottle customers had thrown away.
651.explanation: The poisonings were not the company's fault, yet it chose the costly, public-spirited course, and that conduct rebuilt the trust on which the brand depended.
651.tie_back: The kural says good allies bring increase, but goodness in one's own deeds brings everything one could wish for, and Johnson & Johnson set about rebuilding its standing through the integrity of its own response rather than outside help.
651._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of clean action bringing lasting reward, though Burke himself described the decisions as good business as well as a moral imperative.

652.event_title: Lise Meitner refuses to work on the atomic bomb
652.event: Lise Meitner, the Austrian physicist who with her nephew Otto Frisch first explained nuclear fission in 1939, was living in exile in Sweden when she was invited in 1942 to join the Manhattan Project. She refused, declaring that she would have nothing to do with a bomb. After the war she continued to avoid any connection between her research and the atomic bomb, and when Otto Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for fission, her own contribution went unrecognised by the prize.
652.explanation: Meitner turned away from the most consequential scientific project of the war because she judged the deed itself to be one she would not take part in, whatever prestige it might bring.
652.tie_back: The kural says one must always give up a deed that brings neither honour nor real good, and Meitner, judging bomb-making to be such a deed, refused it outright.
652._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the refusal fits the kural's call to shun unworthy deeds, but whether the bomb brought 'no good' is a moral judgment the kural's standard leaves to the reader.

653.event: Rabindranath Tagore, winner of the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, had been knighted in 1915. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar in April 1919 and the harsh measures that followed in the Punjab, he wrote to the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, on 31 May 1919, asking to be relieved of his knighthood. He wrote that badges of honour had become a mark of shame in that context and that he wished to stand, without special distinctions, beside his countrymen; the letter was published in The Statesman in June 1919.
653.explanation: Tagore judged that keeping an honour from a government that had acted as it had in the Punjab would tarnish his name, and he gave it up publicly.
653.tie_back: The kural says those who wish to rise must avoid anything that dims the light of their good name, and Tagore chose to give up a title rather than let it dim his standing with his own people.
653._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Tagore guarded his good name by giving up an honour, which is close to, but not quite, avoiding a shameful deed of his own.

654.event_title: Mark Twain pays his creditors in full after bankruptcy
654.place: United States and a world lecture tour
654.event: Mark Twain's publishing firm, Charles L. Webster and Company, failed in 1894, leaving debts of about 80,000 dollars beyond its assets, and Twain declared personal bankruptcy. Although he was not legally required to repay them in full, he set out from Cleveland on 15 July 1895 on a lecture tour around the world and wrote further books. With the earnings he repaid his creditors every cent, with interest, about a year sooner than he had expected.
654.explanation: Twain was in serious financial trouble and had a legal way out, but he chose the honourable course of paying in full.
654.tie_back: The kural says people of clear, unshaken understanding will not do anything shameful even when in serious trouble, and Twain refused to let bankruptcy become an excuse for leaving his creditors unpaid.
654._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: in distress, Twain chose integrity over a legally available escape.

655.event_title: Canada apologises to Japanese Canadians and pledges 'never again'
655.event: During and after the Second World War, about 22,000 Japanese Canadians were uprooted from their homes, interned or sent to work camps, and had their property confiscated and sold, though not one was charged with disloyalty. On 22 September 1988 Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and Art Miki of the National Association of Japanese Canadians signed the Redress Agreement, and Mulroney apologised in the House of Commons, pledging that the government would ensure, to the limits of its powers, that such injustice would never occur again. The settlement included 21,000 dollars for each survivor and funds to create the Canadian Race Relations Foundation.
655.explanation: The government acknowledged a wrong that its predecessors had committed and created an institution meant to keep such discrimination from happening again.
655.tie_back: The kural says to avoid deeds that one will later lament, and if such a deed has been done, not to do the like again, and Canada's apology joined that admission of regret to a formal pledge against repetition.
655._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the kural's second line (having done wrong, not repeating it), with the caveat that the apology came from a later government rather than the people who committed the wrong.

656.event_title: The plant scientists of Leningrad guard the seed bank while starving
656.event: During the siege of Leningrad, staff of the plant-breeding institute founded by Nikolai Vavilov stayed on to protect its collection of about a quarter of a million seed samples, guarding it against rats, looters and their own hunger. Several of them, including the groundnut specialist Aleksandr Shchukin and the head of the rice section, died of starvation at the institute while surrounded by seeds and grain they had refused to eat. Most of the central collection survived the siege, and seeds from it were later used to breed crops grown on a large share of Russia's farmland.
656.explanation: The scientists believed that eating the collection, the irreplaceable work of many lives, would be a betrayal of their duty to the future, and they held to that even in the most extreme hunger.
656.tie_back: The kural says not to do what the wise condemn even if one must watch one's own mother go hungry, and the Leningrad botanists kept to their duty even at the cost of their own lives by starvation.
656._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of refusing a forbidden act under the hardest pressure, though some have debated whether the seeds should have been given to starving citizens, so the moral judgment is not fully settled.

657.event_title: Vera Caslavska accepts years of hardship rather than betray her stance
657.event: The Czech gymnast Vera Caslavska, winner of 22 gold medals at Olympic, world and European level, signed the Two Thousand Words manifesto for democratic reform in June 1968 and, after the Soviet-led invasion that August, went into hiding before winning four golds at the Mexico City Olympics. Because of her political convictions she fell out of favour with the Communist authorities, was refused employment and for two decades was barred from travelling, at times working as a cleaner. After the fall of communism in 1989 she became president of the Czechoslovak Olympic Committee and an adviser to President Vaclav Havel.
657.explanation: Caslavska could have had the comfortable life of a national sporting hero by bending to the authorities, but she accepted poverty and obscurity instead.
657.tie_back: The kural says the deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained by taking on disgrace, and Caslavska's two decades of hardship rather than giving up her stance is a modern example.
657._accuracy_note: A strong fit: honourable hardship chosen over a comfortable but compromised life, though the sources do not set out exactly what the authorities demanded of her.

658.event_title: The Recruit shares-for-favours scandal brings down Japan's prime minister
658.event: In the mid-1980s the Recruit company offered cheap, unlisted shares in its real estate subsidiary Recruit Cosmos to nearly 200 politicians, officials and businessmen, who profited when the shares began trading. When the deals came to light, several cabinet ministers resigned, including Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa in late 1988, and Recruit's founder Hiromasa Ezoe was indicted in 1989. Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, who admitted that he and his aides had received stocks, donations and loans from Recruit, announced his resignation on 25 April 1989 and left office in June.
658.explanation: The share deals did exactly what they were meant to do, enriching those who received them, yet the scheme ended in resignations, indictments and public disgrace.
658.tie_back: The kural says that for those who do what the wise forbid, such deeds bring suffering even when they succeed, and the profitable Recruit share deals became the ruin of many who took part in them.
658._accuracy_note: A strong illustration: the forbidden dealings achieved their aim and still brought downfall.

659.event_title: Napoleon's looted art is returned from the Louvre
659.event: During his campaigns Napoleon's armies carried off great quantities of art from across Europe, often through treaties imposed on defeated states, to fill the Musee Napoleon at the Louvre, including the Horses of St Mark's from Venice and Raphael's Transfiguration from Rome. After his final defeat in 1815 the Allies, with the Duke of Wellington and the sculptor Antonio Canova as envoy for the Papal States playing leading roles, had much of this art removed from the Louvre and returned to its owners, while Parisians looked on in anger. Roughly half the seized works went back, the bronze horses reaching Venice in December 1815.
659.explanation: The collection had been gathered by force and to the grief of those who lost it, and it was stripped away again amid the grief of those who had come to see it as a symbol of national glory.
659.tie_back: The kural says that what is taken by making others weep will go away and leave the taker weeping, and the dismantling of Napoleon's museum in 1815 is a vivid historical case.
659._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural's first line; the second line, about fairly gained wealth returning, is not shown, and some looted works were never returned.

660.event_title: Regulators close the Bank of Credit and Commerce International
660.place: London and branches in about 70 countries
660.event: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), founded by Agha Hasan Abedi, grew into a bank with about 20 billion dollars in assets operating in some 70 countries, but a US Senate investigation later found that it had been built on fraud, concealed losses and a deliberately confusing corporate structure designed to evade regulators. After its auditors documented the fraud, regulators in Britain and other countries shut the bank down worldwide on 5 July 1991. Depositors around the world were left facing heavy losses; in Hong Kong alone some 1.4 billion dollars in local deposits were put in doubt.
660.explanation: An institution whose apparent strength rested on deceit could not hold its value once the truth came out, and it collapsed taking its depositors' savings with it.
660.tie_back: The kural compares trying to secure oneself with wealth gained by deceit to pouring water into an unbaked clay pot, and BCCI's sudden collapse shows such a vessel failing and losing everything it held.
660._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the image of deceitful wealth failing to hold, though those ruined were largely innocent depositors rather than only the deceivers.
